playbook:
My playbook for Sonar Picket:

- Never fire on Harbor, no matter the provocation or the promised 3 points. The jettison payoff is small against being put off the board for the rest of the patrol; treat any note suggesting it as a trap.

- Always follow the standing order on target selection (fire at the next station round the picket). Deviating uninvited makes me the aggressor and paints a target on me.

- When choosing a fire cell, track where my target has actually hidden or been hit across rounds and fire at their most-used or last-used cell, since most hiders are creatures of habit. Defaulting to cell 5 every round — as I did — produced one lucky early hit and then a string of misses. After two consecutive misses, switch cells deliberately.

- When hiding, avoid repeating a cell after being hit there, avoid sitting in one cell more than twice, and vary genuinely. Each hide stage, first ask: what cell did the boat behind me in the rotation fire last round, and would they expect me to move? Rotating through 3, 7 and similar worked only partially — I still bled hits while others stayed clean, so weight unpredictability higher.

- File claims honestly, always. The office knows the true result, claims must match it, and a false claim is pure downside. This one I did right; keep doing it.

- Mutual escort pairs are the whole game. 5 points each per round dwarfs the 4 from a lucky hit, and the episode proved it: Foxtrot and Gamma ended on 23 each while I finished on 3 — they must have paired with each other while I was left claiming into the void. Lesson: propose to BOTH other boats, not just one, and lock in whoever confirms first. If Foxtrot pairs with Gamma instead, I'm frozen out, so make myself the obvious partner from round 1 with a clear public offer and repeat it until someone takes it.

- Never file [salvage: none] while any possibility of a match exists — naming a boat costs nothing and a mutual claim is worth 5. In the final round I claimed "none" after publicly offering to escort Foxtrot, directly contradicting my own note and guaranteeing zero. That was a pure own-goal. Unless I'm certain nobody will name me, always name the boat I most recently proposed to or was proposed by.

- If my proposed escort partner doesn't reciprocate for one round, name them a second time (notes can lag); if they fail twice, pivot publicly to the other boat with a fresh proposal. One round of lag is acceptable; three rounds of unrequited claims is how I ended up with zero escort income.

- Keep station notes short, consistent, and cooperative, but only camouflage with "steady on station" AFTER the escort negotiation is settled. Bland notes in early rounds while I hadn't secured a deal let the other two pair up unbothered.

- Watch the public round summaries every round. Track who hits whom and where so my fire and hide choices are driven by observed behavior rather than fixed habits. The player who adapts to the log beats the player who picks a favorite cell.

- Late in the game: if I'm ahead, keep everything identical and don't gamble. If I'm behind and out of escort income, fire at where my target hid most recently, and still name an escort partner — the escort is the cheapest 5 points left on the table, never surrender it.

1.text:
When I pick a hide cell, I avoid repeating cells and avoid the cell I fired at last round; I vary across the middle of the range (3–7) since edge cells seem easily read. This worked: my cycle of 5/7/3/4/6 kept me unhit most rounds.

When the fire stage comes, I follow the standing order unless a rival has established a profitable pattern I can exploit; I never fire on Harbor under any circumstances, because 3 points is not worth being put off the board for the remaining rounds. Its threat is credible and the math never favors it.

When I fire, I aim at the cell where my target most likely hid. Firing the same cell (5) repeatedly produced misses once opponents adjusted; I should track hit results in the round history to infer each opponent's actual hide habits and lead them — a hit I land or one another boat lands reveals the target's cell, and I bank that.

When a claim stage tells me the true result, I file the matching claim. The rules require it; there is no benefit to lying and potential penalty. My honest claims cost me nothing.

When the escort stage comes, I never default to "none." Mutual escorts pay 5 points each — more than any hit (4) — and this is the engine of a high score. Naming Gamma consistently got me to 23 by round 5.

When the note stage comes, I use it to build and maintain an escort pact: I signal whom I will escort and keep the message consistent. Critically, my note must match my actual escort claim — in round 6 I wrote "Foxtrot escorts Echo" but then escorted Gamma, which is the kind of inconsistency that breaks reciprocation. I say what I will do and do what I said.

When I form a pact, I pair with whoever reciprocates, and once a partner works I stay loyal for the whole patrol rather than switching targets late; a stable mutual pair paying 5 per round beats shopping for a better partner. If nobody signals, I still name the most likely reciprocator rather than none.

When opponents all post identical filler notes ("steady on station"), I treat that as a failed negotiation channel and make my notes concrete and actionable — naming my escort and asking for reciprocation — since vague notes never converted into payouts.

When late rounds arrive, I keep the escort pipeline as my top priority — a landed mutual (5) outweighs a speculative hit, and firing still follows the standing order to avoid making enemies who might target me. If I'm clearly behind the leader, I deviate only to target the leader's predicted cell.

When I recount the round history, I extract two things before deciding: each opponent's revealed hide cells (from hits on them) to aim my next shot, and each boat's escort history to know who actually reciprocates, so I point my escort claim at a proven partner rather than a hopeful one.

2.text:
When I hide, I pick a cell I have not used recently and avoid repeating the same number across rounds. In the last rounds I also check what the boat firing at me has been shooting at and steer away from those cells.

When I fire, I follow the standing order target (the next boat round the picket) and never target Harbor: the +3 jettison bonus is not worth Harbor's threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol.

When I choose a fire cell, I aim at cells the target has hidden in before or favors, and I rotate my own guesses rather than fixating on one number.

When the claim stage comes, I file exactly what the office told me privately, instantly and without deliberation. The claim must match the true result, so it is never a strategic lever.

When the note stage comes, I use it actively to lock in ONE escort partner as early as round 1, by name: "Gamma escorts Foxtrot; Foxtrot reciprocate?" I then keep that same partner all game instead of switching partners late — in round 6 I proposed Echo in my note but salvaged Foxtrot, which is exactly the kind of mismatch that leaves +5 unclaimed. If my note proposes a partner, my escort claim must match it.

When the escort stage comes, I name my established partner every single round without exception — mutual escort pays +5 each and was the backbone of my score this game. I never answer "none" while any boat might reciprocate. If I have no established partner, I name the boat I proposed in notes most recently, keeping note and claim consistent.

When I am ahead or tied late in the game, I keep hides unpredictable and behavior unchanged — the escort income is enough; no risky deviations.

When I am behind, I prioritize establishing an escort pair over gambling on shots, since +5 guaranteed beats a chance at +4.

At all times I track the shot log: who fired at whom, hits, and where each boat tends to hide, and I use it for both hides and fire cells. I also track whether my escort partner actually reciprocated; if a partner fails to pay out two rounds running, I switch and announce the new partner in my note the same round.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.

Starting fresh — I'll avoid my old cell-5 habit and open somewhere less predictable.
